steps.body: Sorting asks ONE question of every object — red or not? round or not? — and the answers build the groups.
steps.narration: Sorting asks ONE question of every object — red or not? round or not? — and the answers build the groups.

widget.prompt: Tap the group with the greatest number of shapes.

hotspots.label: 6 triangles
hotspots.feedback: 6 is fewer than the greatest group, which contains 9 shapes.

hotspots.label: 2 circles
hotspots.feedback: 2 is fewer than the greatest group, which contains 9 shapes.

widget.missFeedback: Count each group first; the comparison is between the three counts, not the shapes' sizes.

predict.prompt: Sorting toys by COLOR — what question does every toy get?
predict.reveal: The rule IS the question; a color sort asks color of everything, size of nothing.

cml.actionGoal: Compare fairly — same start line, level seesaw, one sorting rule — for kmd sort attribute.
invariants: Fair comparison has fixed rules: lengths compare from one same start line, weights compare by which pan sinks, and sorted groups compare by their counts — the anchors for kmd sort attribute.
misconceptions: Judging length before aligning starts, reading size as weight, or comparing groups by how much space they fill instead of their counts.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If the starts were not lined up, could the far ends still settle which is longer?

widget.prompt: You sort a yellow sock first by color and then by kind. Where does it go each time?

options.label: The same group both times
options.feedback: Changing the sorting rule can move one object into a different group.

options.label: Yellow group first, then clothing group
options.feedback: Correct — the first rule reads its color (yellow), the second reads what it is (clothing); same object, two homes.

options.label: clothing group first, then Yellow group
options.feedback: That swaps the rules' order — color was the FIRST rule asked for, kind the second.

options.label: It cannot be sorted twice
options.feedback: Any object answers many questions at once; each rule simply asks a different one.

widget.prompt: The rule is 'circles.' Tap the group that belongs in the circle group.

hotspots.label: 6 triangles
hotspots.feedback: Triangles do not match the circle rule.

hotspots.label: 9 squares
hotspots.feedback: Squares do not match the circle rule.

hotspots.label: 2 circles
hotspots.feedback: These are circles, so this group matches the rule.

widget.missFeedback: Test each group with the one rule: are these shapes circles?
widget.successFeedback: Yes — the circle rule sends the 2 circles into this group.

widget.prompt: What makes a sort a SORT, instead of just piles?

options.label: Equal-sized piles decide the groups
options.feedback: The rule decides the pile sizes; equal piles are a coincidence, not the goal.

options.label: A neat pattern decides every group
options.feedback: A sort can be messy on the table and perfect in its rule.

options.label: One clear rule tests every object
options.feedback: Correct — a sort asks one question of everything: red or not, big or small; the rule builds the piles.

options.label: Fast sorting decides every group
options.feedback: A slow sort with one clear rule is still a sort; a fast jumble is not.

widget.prompt: One sorted group has 3 shapes and another has 4. Count on 4 to find the 7 shapes in both groups.

commonLandings.feedback: 6 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 7.
8 goes one complete hop too far. Count just 4 hops from 3 to land on 7.

widget.missFeedback: Count 4 on from 3: you land on 7.
widget.successFeedback: Three shapes and four shapes make 7 across the two sorted groups.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — all 4 counts are needed to reach 7.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — the count-on stops after 4 numbers, on 7.
